HIPPOCRATES_PROGNOSTIC_II.work: Hippocratic Prognostic, complete Internet Classics Archive Part 2
HIPPOCRATES_PROGNOSTIC_II.historical_date: Ancient Greek work, conventionally around400BCE as the institutional host labels it; precise authorship/date and a medieval Latin witness are not established here.
HIPPOCRATES_PROGNOSTIC_II.witness: Francis Adams English translation (1849 tradition), MIT Internet Classics Archive digital text. This task owns this complete English section, not a Greek manuscript or medieval Latin wording.
HIPPOCRATES_PROGNOSTIC_II.catalog_limit: Perseus catalog identifies Adams,1886 printing, originally1849; it does not prove the exact print exemplar used by the MIT page.
HIPPOCRATES_PROGNOSTIC_II.normalization: HTML text only, whitespace collapsed, one final newline; whole Part2 bounded from He should observe thus to lips ... blanched. No OCR or image inspection.
HIPPOCRATES_PROGNOSTIC_II.full_text: He should observe thus in acute diseases: first, the countenance of the patient, if it be like those of persons in health, and more so, if like itself, for this is the best of all; whereas the most opposite to it is the worst, such as the following; a sharp nose, hollow eyes, collapsed temples; the ears cold, contracted, and their lobes turned out: the skin about the forehead being rough, distended, and parched; the color of the whole face being green, black, livid, or lead-colored. If the countenance be such at the commencement of the disease, and if this cannot be accounted for from the other symptoms, inquiry must be made whether the patient has long wanted sleep; whether his bowels have been very loose; and whether he has suffered from want of food; and if any of these causes be confessed to, the danger is to be reckoned so far less; and it becomes obvious, in the course of a day and a night, whether or not the appearance of the countenance proceeded from these causes. But if none of these be said to exist, if the symptoms do not subside in the aforesaid time, it is to be known for certain that death is at hand. And, also, if the disease be in a more advanced stage either on the third or fourth day, and the countenance be such, the same inquiries as formerly directed are to be made, and the other symptoms are to be noted, those in the whole countenance, those on the body, and those in the eyes; for if they shun the light, or weep involuntarily, or squint, or if the one be less than the other, or if the white of them be red, livid, or has black veins in it; if there be a gum upon the eyes, if they are restless, protruding, or are become very hollow; and if the countenance be squalid and dark, or the color of the whole face be changed- all these are to be reckoned bad and fatal symptoms. The physician should also observe the appearance of the eyes from below the eyelids in sleep; for when a portion of the white appears, owing to the eyelids not being closed together, and when this is not connected with diarrhea or purgation from medicine, or when the patient does not sleep thus from habit, it is to be reckoned an unfavorable and very deadly symptom; but if the eyelid be contracted, livid, or pale, or also the lip, or nose, along with some of the other symptoms, one may know for certain that death is close at hand. It is a mortal symptom, also, when the lips are relaxed, pendent, cold, and blanched.

complete_inventory.content: In acute disease examine the countenance first. Similarity to healthy people is favorable, similarity to the patient’s own healthy appearance more favorable; the most opposed appearance is worst.

Retain the full adverse-face description: sharp nose; hollow eyes; collapsed temples; cold contracted ears with turned-out lobes; rough, distended and parched forehead skin; whole-face color green, black, livid or lead-colored.
At disease onset, if that appearance is not accounted for by other symptoms, inquire about prolonged sleeplessness, very loose bowels and lack of food.
If any of those causes is admitted, danger is judged less. A day and night makes apparent whether the countenance arose from these causes. Reduced danger does not mean guaranteed survival.

The two written if-clauses concern none of those causes being reported and symptoms not subsiding in the aforementioned interval, followed by imminent-death prognosis. Their exact conjunction/scope is not silently resolved from this English translation.

At the more advanced third or fourth day with the same appearance, repeat the same inquiries and attend to other signs on the whole face, body and eyes. This is a genuine backward procedural reference, not a new independent question list.

Keep every further adverse sign: eyes shunning light, involuntary tears, squint, unequal size, red or livid whites or black veins, gum, restlessness, protrusion or marked hollowness; a squalid dark countenance or changed whole-face color. The passage calls these bad and fatal.

Observe eyes during sleep: exposed white because lids do not close, with written exclusions mentioning diarrhea, medicinal purgation and the patient’s habitual sleep appearance. Preserve the printed and/or connective ambiguity; do not silently replace it with a medical rule preferred by the analyst.
Contracted, livid or pale eyelid, lip or nose together with some other signs entails imminent death in the source’s historical claim.
The final separate assertion calls relaxed, pendent, cold and blanched lips a mortal sign. Do not omit it merely because the first temporal contrast supplied the proposed discriminator.

source_ambiguities: The paired if-clauses before imminent death do not receive an unannounced Boolean connective.
The eyelid passage prints and/or around diarrhea, medicinal purgation and habit. A Greek/edition collation is required before a unique truth table is selected.
The source’s comparative danger, fatal, very deadly and imminent-death judgments are not collapsed to one binary output.
Healthy-person comparison and this patient’s own healthy baseline are distinct.
Historical prognoses are source claims, not current medical guidance.

PHAEDRUS_I1.work: Phaedrus, Fabulae I.1, Lupus et Agnus, complete15-line fable
PHAEDRUS_I1.historical_date: Roman imperial Latin work conventionally attributed to first-centuryCE Phaedrus; no medieval manuscript was collated in this task.
PHAEDRUS_I1.witness: IntraText Latin digital text. Its exact printed-edition ancestry is not established here. A Perseus1876Mueller search record was only a navigation comparator; its text endpoint and attempted XML fetch failed and are not claimed as the owned edition.
PHAEDRUS_I1.normalization: HTML text only, whitespace collapsed, one final newline; complete from Ad rivum eundem through qui fictis causis innocentes opprimunt. Fifteen verse lines retained as conventional locators in the inventory, not target boundaries.
PHAEDRUS_I1.full_text: Ad rivum eundem lupus et agnus venerant, siti compulsi. Superior stabat lupus, longeque inferior agnus. Tunc fauce improba latro incitatus iurgii causam intulit; 'Cur' inquit 'turbulentam fecisti mihi aquam bibenti?' Laniger contra timens 'Qui possum, quaeso, facere quod quereris, lupe? A te decurrit ad meos haustus liquor'. Repulsus ille veritatis viribus 'Ante hos sex menses male' ait 'dixisti mihi'. Respondit agnus 'Equidem natus non eram'. 'Pater hercle tuus' ille inquit 'male dixit mihi'; atque ita correptum lacerat iniusta nece. Haec propter illos scripta est homines fabula qui fictis causis innocentes opprimunt.

complete_inventory.content: The wolf and lamb reach the same stream because of thirst; wolf stands above, lamb far below. Same stream is not a claim that one indivisible water portion is reused.
Narrator calls the wolf a robber and gives fauce improba as the motive for starting a quarrel. Ravenous/malicious appetite is an interpretation; the expression is preserved in the Latin.
Wolf alleges the lamb has muddied the water for him while he drinks. The question carries an accusation, not an authorial assertion that muddying occurred.
The fearful wool-bearer, identified as the lamb by continuity, asks how that is possible: water flows from the wolf to the lamb’s drinking place. The flow objection concerns causal direction.
Narrator says the wolf was repulsed by the force of truth; this licenses endorsement of the rebuttal within the story.
Wolf alleges a verbal offense against himself six months earlier.
Lamb answers that it had not yet been born; temporal existence is the second, independent prerequisite for the alleged action.

Wolf substitutes the lamb’s father as alleged offender. Father is a new participant related to the lamb, not a pronoun or synonym for the lamb. No reply establishes whether the father actually offended.
Wolf seizes and tears the lamb in an unjust killing. A completed violent outcome does not turn the earlier charges into facts.
The narrator explicitly says the fable is written against people who oppress the innocent with invented causes. The general moral and authorial purpose belong to the complete content.

source_ambiguities: The father accusation is reported but not separately verified or refuted.
Water/liquor names a flowing medium; no conservation or whole-portion identity is asserted.
The spatial impossibility is the story’s endorsed causal reasoning, not a new hydraulic experiment.
Narrator, wolf, lamb and father are distinct discourse roles; moral oppressors and innocents generalize the story rather than introducing extra on-scene animals.
Verse form, capitalization and punctuation do not license a Voynich writer or a fixed group count.
